title: Choose a realtime transport for each feature
objective: Pick polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events or WebSocket for a product feature and justify the choice by data direction and tolerated delay.
summary: A branching deck compares periodic polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSocket by who sends the data and how much delay is acceptable, shows the bandwidth cost of short polling intervals, and opens four deep dives: a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.

checkpoints.prompt: 10,000 clients poll every 60 seconds and get no new messages. They switch to every 1 second. What happens to the traffic the server receives?

choices.text: It rises about 60 times, to over 60 Mbps
It stays about the same, because the responses are empty
choices.misconception: Thinks an empty poll is free; each request still carries about 850 bytes of headers and cookies

choices.text: It falls, because each response gets smaller
choices.misconception: Confuses response size with request count; the number of requests grows with every shorter interval

checkpoints.explanation: Each empty check still costs about 850 bytes of HTTP overhead. Sixty times more requests give about sixty times more traffic, so short intervals are expensive.

checkpoints.prompt: A collaborative cursor sends and receives positions many times a second. Why is Server-Sent Events the wrong choice?

choices.text: The client cannot send data on an SSE connection after the handshake
SSE delivers each message with a long delay
choices.misconception: Thinks SSE is slow; SSE pushes each message the moment the server has it
Confuses SSE with a non-HTTP protocol; an SSE stream is a normal HTTP response and can use TLS

checkpoints.explanation: SSE is server-to-client only. The cursor must also send the user's own position, and WebSocket is the transport that carries messages both ways on one connection.

checkpoints.prompt: A dashboard ticker gets many price updates per second, but it may show prices that are up to 30 seconds old. Which transport makes the fewest requests?

choices.misconception: Thinks long polling always makes fewer requests; at a high update rate it opens a new request after every update
Thinks a shorter interval is always better; it adds requests the dashboard does not need

checkpoints.explanation: When some delay is acceptable and updates arrive often, periodic polling collects many updates into one response. Long polling ends after each update, so a high rate means many requests.
